rule: Docs and newsfragment prose must use the Airflow 3 spellings of core nouns: `Dag`, `Dag run`, `Dag files`, `Dag bundles`, `Dag Processor`, `API Server` (never `DAG`, `webserver`, or `DAG processor`), while generic concept words stay lowercase (`email notifier`, not `email Notifier`) unless they name an actual class
trigger: A `.rst` docs page or newsfragment adds prose containing `DAG`, `DAG run`, `DAG files`, `webserver`, `DAG processor`, or capitalises a generic concept noun that is not a class name
rationale: Airflow 3 renamed the components and standardised on `Dag` in prose; mixed spellings in new pages make them inconsistent with the rest of the documentation, and capitalising a concept implies a class that does not exist

evidence.excerpt: Deadline Alerts allow you to set time thresholds for your Dag runs

rule: When docs enumerate a feature's parameters, each bullet must name the exact keyword argument in double backticks (``reference``, ``interval``, ``callback``) and the stated mandatory/optional counts must match the real signature
trigger: A docs page lists parameters as capitalised prose words (`Reference:`, `Interval:`, `Callback Kwargs:`) or claims a number of mandatory parameters that disagrees with the constructor signature
rationale: Readers copy parameter names straight from the docs into their Dag code, so prose names that differ from the real keyword arguments produce examples that cannot run

evidence.excerpt: looks more like 3 mandatory args but we can modify callback

rule: `curl` examples in the docs must percent-encode reserved characters in the query string (`%7C` for `|`, `%5E` for `^`) or use `curl --data-urlencode`, so the example runs when copied verbatim
trigger: A `.. code-block:: bash` block adds a curl invocation whose URL query string contains a raw `|`, `^`, or other RFC 3986 reserved character
rationale: `|` and `^` are not valid URL characters and may be rejected by proxies and clients, so the copy/pasted API example fails for the reader

evidence.excerpt: `|` is not a valid URL character per RFC 3986

rule: A language-SDK docs page that documents log forwarding must also document the configuration the SDK already reads for it — for the Java SDK, `AIRFLOW__LOGGING__LOGGING_LEVEL` and `AIRFLOW__LOGGING__NAMESPACE_LEVELS`
trigger: A new Logging section under `airflow-core/docs/authoring-and-scheduling/language-sdks/` lists the integration artifacts but has no subsection on setting log levels
rationale: The Java side reads those env vars at startup; documenting only the artifacts leaves users unable to discover configuration that already exists

evidence.excerpt: reads AIRFLOW__LOGGING__LOGGING_LEVEL and AIRFLOW__LOGGING__NAMESPACE_LEVELS at startup - worth a short subsection

rule: A new row in `extra-packages-ref.rst` must describe exactly the component types the provider ships (hooks, triggers, queue providers, operators); do not write "hooks and operators" for a provider that defines no operators
trigger: A diff adds a row to the extras table in `airflow-core/docs/extra-packages-ref.rst` whose description does not match the components actually defined in the corresponding provider package
rationale: The extras table is how users decide which extra to install; a description that overstates what a provider ships sends them hunting for operators that do not exist

evidence.excerpt: provider currently defines hooks/triggers/queue provider and no operators

rule: A PR's title and description must describe the scope actually present in the diff; a documentation/CI/repo-metadata-only change must not be titled as a CLI or behaviour fix
trigger: PR title or description claims a code/CLI behaviour change (e.g. "map_index bounds validation") but the diff touches only docs, CI configuration, or repo metadata
rationale: Airflow's changelog tooling and reviewers both work from the title and description, so a mismatch misleads the release notes as well as the review

evidence.excerpt: update the PR title/description to reflect the documentation/CI scope to avoid misleading changelog tooling

rule: `AsyncCallback` must wrap something that is actually awaitable; synchronous notifiers such as `SlackWebhookNotifier` expose no awaitables and must not appear inside `AsyncCallback` in deadline-alert examples or Dag code
trigger: `AsyncCallback(` is constructed with a notifier or callable that defines no async interface, in docs examples or in deadline configuration
rationale: Docs examples are copied verbatim, so pairing AsyncCallback with a non-awaitable notifier ships an example that cannot work; reviewers insist examples be working examples

evidence.excerpt: This should be awaitable for `AsyncCallback`, SlackWebhookNotifier doesn't have any awaitbale's

rule: Do not describe the Execution API as an "internal" API; describe it as an API for use by Airflow itself rather than third-party callers, because it is deliberately reachable from outside the deployment
trigger: Security or API documentation introduces the Execution API with the word "internal", or implies it is not exposed outside the deployment boundary
rationale: Calling it internal suggests to deployers that it need not be secured or exposed, but workers call it from outside the deployment

evidence.excerpt: clarify what we mean by "internal" -- since it is designed to be called

rule: The UI authentication JWT must be stored in a secure, HTTP-only `_token` cookie with `SameSite=Lax`, never in browser local storage or local settings
trigger: Auth-manager or UI code, or documentation of it, stores or describes storing the `access_token` anywhere other than the secure HTTP-only cookie
rationale: The project deliberately moved off local settings/storage to secure cookies because local storage is vulnerable to a wider class of attacks

evidence.excerpt: we changed it later to securit cookies, as Local Setting are portentially vulnerable

rule: Execution API JWTs are minted by the scheduler via the executor's `jwt_generator` property while the workload is built; `executor.queue_workload()` must not generate tokens, it forwards whatever workload it is given
trigger: An executor implementation creates or refreshes a task JWT inside `queue_workload()` (or elsewhere in the executor) instead of consuming the token already present on the workload
rationale: Token minting is centralised on the scheduler side so every executor produces identical tokens configured from `[execution_api]`, and executors stay dumb transports

evidence.excerpt: `executor.queue_workload()` doesn't do the generation, it just takes what ever it is given

rule: Security-model guidance that narrows credential distribution must keep connection credentials available to the Dag processor and triggerer; only the JWT signing key is withheld from components that neither generate nor validate tokens (workers)
trigger: `security_model.rst` or deployment guidance adds advice that connection credentials should be available only to the API server, without carving out the Dag processor and triggerer
rationale: The triggerer needs connections for async jobs (e.g. Databricks) and the Dag processor needs them for deadline-alert notifiers (e.g. Slack); a blanket restriction disables those features

evidence.excerpt: if you don't allow Conns to the DagFileProcessor or Trigger it will severely limit

rule: A `.feature.rst` newsfragment must state what the new API does for users, not the internal defect it fixes: "check whether a user is authorized to approve a HITL task", not "to fix ApprovalOperator authorization"
trigger: A newsfragment sentence is phrased as "... to fix <internal component/behaviour>" instead of describing the capability the change adds
rationale: Newsfragments become release notes read by operators who never saw the bug, so fix-framing tells them nothing about what changed for them

evidence.excerpt: method to check whether a user a is authorized to approve a HITL task

rule: A `.significant.rst` newsfragment that ticks the Behaviour-change or Code-interface-change checkbox must spell out the delta in prose: "Previously it worked as X, now it works as Y" / "Previously the interface was X, now it is Y"
trigger: A `.significant.rst` file marks `[x] Behaviour changes` or `[x] Code interface changes` but contains no before/after explanation of what changed
rationale: The ticked checkbox alone does not tell an upgrading user what to change; the explicit before/after is what makes the fragment actionable

rule: A significant newsfragment describing an observability or process-management change must add the operator-visible impact and migration step (dashboards built on the old Gauge must move to Histogram aggregations; how to roll-restart the api-server on Kubernetes)
trigger: A `.significant.rst` describes an internal representation or process change (metric instrument type, uvicorn worker/restart model) without saying what existing deployments must do about it
rationale: Operators read these fragments to decide whether their Grafana panels or deployment automation break; the internal description alone leaves that unknown

rule: Do not add a newsfragment for a documentation-only change; a `.doc.rst` fragment for a pure docs update is overkill
trigger: A PR whose diff touches only files under `docs/` also adds a file under `airflow-core/newsfragments/`
rationale: Docs updates do not need release-note entries, and the extra fragment adds review and changelog noise for no reader benefit

rule: Partition mapper classes must be named `To<Granularity>Mapper` (`ToHourlyMapper`, `ToDailyMapper`, `ToWeeklyMapper`, `ToMonthlyMapper`, `ToQuarterlyMapper`), not the bare granularity name
trigger: A new partition mapper class, or documentation of one, uses a bare granularity name such as `HourlyMapper` or `DailyMapper`
rationale: Mappers transform upstream partition keys into a different granularity, so the `To` prefix makes the direction of the transform explicit rather than ambiguous

evidence.excerpt: ``ToHourlyMapper``, ``ToDailyMapper``, ``ToWeeklyMapper``, ``ToMonthlyMapper``, ``ToQuarterlyMapper``

rule: Profiling and other developer-only libraries (e.g. `memray`) must be declared as an optional extra in `airflow-core/pyproject.toml`, never appended to the mandatory `dependencies` list
trigger: A diff adds an entry to the top-level `dependencies = [...]` array in `airflow-core/pyproject.toml` for a tool that only some users need
rationale: Every mandatory dependency is installed for every Airflow user; opt-in tooling belongs behind an extra such as `pip install 'apache-airflow[memray]'`

rule: Cross-team asset-event triggering must ship with the most restrictive default (a teamless API user may trigger only teamless consumers) and the restriction must be documented with the reasoning behind it
trigger: Multi-team documentation or code defines which producers may trigger which consumers across team boundaries, and either proposes a permissive default or states a rule with no explanation
rationale: Reviewers prefer shipping with more restrictions and relaxing them later if needed; a permissive cross-team default cannot be tightened without a breaking change

rule: In `multi-team.rst`, feature-specific sections belong above the concluding multi-team architecture diagram, which is meant to end the page
trigger: A new section is appended after the `multi_team_arch_diagram.png` image block in `airflow-core/docs/core-concepts/multi-team.rst`
rationale: The overall architecture diagram is the generic conclusion of the page, so a specifically targeted section placed after it buries the new content
